about.title: Palmdale Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Palmdale sits at the high-desert end of Los Angeles County, and its wide boulevards move a lot of cars at speed. In 2025, public records logged 815 injury collisions inside the city, with 1,231 people hurt and 14 lives lost. Palmdale Boulevard, Rancho Vista Boulevard, Avenue S and Sierra Highway account for the largest share of those reports, and Friday evenings between 5 and 7 p.m. show the heaviest cluster. Behind each number is someone dealing with a totaled vehicle, missed shifts and an adjuster who calls before the tow bill even arrives. LawProactive exists for that moment. We are not a law firm. We are a free service that matches you with an independent personal injury attorney who handles car accident claims and works on contingency, so nothing comes out of your pocket unless money is recovered. Your job is to get treated and hold onto photos, repair estimates and medical paperwork. The attorney's job is to deal with the insurer on your behalf so you can focus on healing.

whyChoose.title: Why Palmdale Drivers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: The clock in California is real
items.desc: You generally have two years to file a car accident lawsuit, but if a city or county vehicle or road condition is involved, the window can shrink to six months. An attorney can sort out which deadline applies before it slips by.

items.title: Partial fault does not shut you out
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover even if you share some blame; your share simply reduces the amount. That matters in disputed intersection crashes along Rancho Vista Boulevard where both drivers point fingers.

items.title: Free to connect, contingency to hire
items.desc: LawProactive never charges you, and the independent attorneys in our network take car accident cases on contingency. There is no legal fee unless there is a recovery, and California places no cap on pain and suffering damages in ordinary car crash claims.

items.question: The other driver's insurance company wants a recorded statement about my Sierra Highway crash. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually wise not to. Adjusters are trained to ask questions that can later be used to shrink your claim. Let an attorney handle those conversations and share only what is legally required.

items.question: I was hit on a Friday evening on Palmdale Boulevard and never got a police report. Can I still make a claim?
items.answer: Yes. A police report helps, but it is not required to pursue a claim. Photos of the vehicles and scene, names of witnesses, your medical records and any dash-cam footage can all establish what happened. The sooner that evidence is gathered, the stronger your position.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the collision?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule lets you recover damages even when you share responsibility; your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you were found 20 percent responsible, you could still recover 80 percent of your losses. An attorney can push back on inflated fault assignments from the insurer.
